lessonTitle: Chronic Kidney Disease and Glomerular Syndromes

blocks.text: A 27-year-old man notices his face is puffy in the morning, his ankles swell by evening and his urine foams in the toilet bowl. His blood pressure is normal and a dipstick shows 4+ protein but no blood. Compare him with a different young adult whose urine is the colour of weak tea and whose blood pressure is 165/100: both have glomerular disease, but the two syndromes are very different.

blocks.markdown: The glomerulus is a filter with three layers: fenestrated endothelium, the glomerular basement membrane (GBM) and the podocyte slit diaphragm. Size and charge selectivity keep albumin and red cells in the blood. When the filter is damaged by **inflammation**, red cells and some protein leak and filtration falls (a **nephritic** picture). When the podocyte barrier is damaged without much inflammation, albumin leaks in large amounts (a **nephrotic** picture). If damage persists, nephrons are lost progressively and **chronic kidney disease (CKD)** results.

blocks.title: Chronic kidney disease
blocks.text: CKD is abnormal kidney structure or function, present for more than 3 months, with implications for health. It is classified by cause, by glomerular filtration rate category (G1 to G5) and by albuminuria category (A1 to A3). Estimated GFR (eGFR) is calculated by the laboratory from serum creatinine, age and sex, and is expressed in mL/min/1.73 m2.

blocks.caption: CKD classification (KDIGO/NICE). G1 and G2 count as CKD only if there is other evidence of kidney damage such as albuminuria or structural abnormality. Thresholds are guideline-based.
Albumin:creatinine ratio on a spot urine, which corrects for how dilute the urine is.

blocks.title: Staging a CKD patient
blocks.prompt: A patient has an eGFR of 38 mL/min/1.73 m2 on two samples four months apart. A spot urine has albumin 200 mg/L and creatinine 8 mmol/L. Give the CKD stage.

steps.text: Chronicity: abnormal results more than 3 months apart satisfy the time criterion.
GFR category: 38 lies between 30 and 44, so G3b.

blocks.markdown: **Nephritic versus nephrotic syndrome.** The nephritic syndrome is inflammatory: haematuria (often with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts), hypertension, reduced GFR with oliguria, and usually modest proteinuria. Examples include post-infectious glomerulonephritis, IgA nephropathy, anti-GBM disease and ANCA-associated vasculitis. The nephrotic syndrome is defined by heavy proteinuria (above 3.5 g per day), hypoalbuminaemia (below about 30 g/L), oedema, and usually hyperlipidaemia. Causes include minimal change disease (the commonest in children), membranous nephropathy and focal segmental glomerulosclerosis in adults, and diabetic nephropathy. Because albumin and clotting inhibitors leak into urine, nephrotic patients are at risk of venous thrombosis and infection.

rows: Haematuria, red cell casts, modest protein
Marked, from low albumin and salt retention
blocks.caption: Distinguishing glomerular syndromes.

blocks.title: Is it nephrotic range?
blocks.prompt: A patient collects urine for 24 hours: volume 2.0 L, protein 2.2 g/L. Serum albumin is 24 g/L. Is this nephrotic-range proteinuria?

steps.text: Total protein is concentration multiplied by volume.
The nephrotic threshold is above 3.5 g per day, and 4.4 exceeds it.
Serum albumin of 24 g/L is also below about 30 g/L, which fits the syndrome. Add oedema and the picture is nephrotic.

items: Fluid and salt retention, hypertension and cardiovascular disease, the leading cause of death in CKD.
Hyperkalaemia and metabolic acidosis as the kidney loses the ability to excrete potassium and acid.
Anaemia of CKD from reduced erythropoietin (normocytic), treated after iron correction with erythropoiesis-stimulating agents.
CKD mineral and bone disorder: reduced 1-alpha hydroxylation of vitamin D, hyperphosphataemia and low calcium cause secondary hyperparathyroidism and renal bone disease.
Uraemic symptoms at advanced stages: nausea, itching, fatigue, pericarditis, encephalopathy.

blocks.title: Renal replacement options
blocks.text: When kidney failure is reached (usually G5, or earlier with symptoms), options are haemodialysis (typically three sessions weekly), peritoneal dialysis (daily, at home, using the peritoneum as the membrane), kidney transplantation (best long-term survival and quality of life in suitable patients) or conservative care without dialysis in frail patients who prefer it.

points: CKD is a structural or functional abnormality persisting over 3 months, staged by eGFR (G1 to G5) and ACR (A1 to A3).
Nephritic syndrome is inflammatory with haematuria, hypertension and falling GFR; nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria, hypoalbuminaemia and oedema.
Advanced CKD causes anaemia, bone mineral disease, hyperkalaemia, acidosis, hypertension and uraemia.
Replacement therapies are haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis and transplantation, or conservative care.

questions.stem: A man has eGFR 52 mL/min/1.73 m2 on tests four months apart and a urine albumin:creatinine ratio of 2 mg/mmol. Which CKD category applies?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: eGFR 45 to 59 is G3a and ACR under 3 is A1.
distractorRationale.c: G3b requires eGFR 30 to 44 and A2 requires ACR 3 to 30.

questions.explanation: The GFR category is read from the eGFR band and the albuminuria category from the ACR band. An eGFR below 60 for more than 3 months is CKD regardless of albuminuria.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old develops dark urine 2 days after a sore throat. BP is 158/96 mmHg, urine output is reduced, and urine microscopy shows red cell casts. Which syndrome is this?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: haematuria, red cell casts, hypertension and oliguria define nephritic syndrome.
distractorRationale.b: Nephrotic syndrome is heavy proteinuria with little haematuria and often normal BP.
distractorRationale.c: Obstruction does not produce red cell casts.
distractorRationale.d: Prerenal states have a bland sediment.

questions.explanation: Red cell casts show bleeding from the glomerulus itself, which is a marker of glomerular inflammation. Together with hypertension and oliguria this is the nephritic picture, and a recent infection suggests a post-infectious or IgA-related cause.

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy has periorbital oedema, frothy urine, serum albumin 18 g/L, normal blood pressure, and urine dipstick with 4+ protein and no blood. Which is the most likely diagnosis?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the commonest cause of nephrotic syndrome in children.
distractorRationale.b: Vasculitis causes a nephritic picture with haematuria.
distractorRationale.c: Anti-GBM disease is a nephritic, rapidly progressive illness.
distractorRationale.d: Diabetic nephropathy follows years of diabetes and is rare in a 5-year-old.

questions.explanation: Heavy proteinuria, low albumin, oedema and a bland urine without haematuria or hypertension make this nephrotic syndrome. Minimal change disease is the commonest cause in children and typically responds to corticosteroids.

questions.stem: A patient with eGFR 18 mL/min/1.73 m2 has haemoglobin 88 g/L with normal MCV, normal ferritin and low reticulocytes. What is the principal mechanism of the anaemia?

options.text: Reduced erythropoietin production by the kidney

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced erythropoietin production by the kidney

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the failing kidney makes too little erythropoietin.
distractorRationale.d: Erythropoietin is reduced, not increased, in CKD.

questions.explanation: Renal interstitial cells produce erythropoietin, so advanced CKD causes a normocytic, hypoproliferative anaemia. Iron stores are checked and corrected first, then erythropoiesis-stimulating agents are used.

questions.stem: A patient with advanced CKD has high phosphate, low calcium and a raised PTH. Which explanation best accounts for the raised PTH?

options.text: Reduced vitamin D activation and phosphate retention lowering calcium and stimulating the parathyroid glands
A parathyroid adenoma that is autonomous of calcium

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced vitamin D activation and phosphate retention lowering calcium and stimulating the parathyroid glands

distractorRationale.a: Correct: this is secondary hyperparathyroidism of CKD.
distractorRationale.b: An adenoma causes primary hyperparathyroidism with high calcium.
distractorRationale.c: Excess vitamin D would raise calcium and suppress PTH.
distractorRationale.d: Calcium reabsorption is not increased in this setting.

questions.explanation: The failing kidney cannot make active vitamin D (calcitriol) and retains phosphate, both of which lower serum calcium. The parathyroid glands respond with a raised PTH, which in the long run causes renal bone disease.

questions.stem: A spot urine has albumin 90 mg/L and creatinine 6 mmol/L. Calculate the albumin:creatinine ratio in mg/mmol.
questions.explanation: ACR is albumin divided by creatinine, 90 / 6 = 15 mg/mmol. This lies between 3 and 30 and so is albuminuria category A2.

questions.stem: A patient with oedema collects urine for 24 hours: volume 1.6 L with a protein concentration of 2.8 g/L. Calculate the 24-hour protein excretion in g/day.
questions.explanation: Total protein is concentration multiplied by volume: 2.8 g/L x 1.6 L = 4.48 g/day. This exceeds 3.5 g/day so it is nephrotic-range proteinuria, and with low albumin and oedema supports nephrotic syndrome.

questions.stem: Compare the presentation and urine findings of nephritic and nephrotic syndromes, giving one example cause of each.
markingGuide: Nephritic: haematuria with red cell casts, hypertension, oliguria, reduced GFR
Nephrotic: heavy proteinuria over 3.5 g/day, hypoalbuminaemia, oedema, hyperlipidaemia
Nephrotic: little or no haematuria, BP often normal
Example nephritic cause such as IgA nephropathy, post-infectious or ANCA vasculitis
Example nephrotic cause such as minimal change, membranous or diabetic nephropathy
questions.explanation: Nephritic syndrome is driven by glomerular inflammation, giving blood in the urine, hypertension and a falling GFR. Nephrotic syndrome is driven by loss of the filtration barrier to albumin, giving heavy proteinuria and oedema with relatively little blood.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with diabetic kidney disease reaches eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73 m2. Describe the complications you would anticipate and the options for renal replacement.
markingGuide: Hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism (renal bone disease)
Options: haemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, transplantation, conservative care
Transplantation gives best outcomes in suitable patients
questions.explanation: At eGFR below 15 the kidney can no longer excrete potassium, acid, water and phosphate or make erythropoietin and active vitamin D, which explains the complications. Replacement therapy substitutes for these functions, with transplantation offering the best long-term outcome when the patient is suitable.

questions.stem: True or false: a patient with a persistent eGFR of 70 mL/min/1.73 m2, no albuminuria and normal renal imaging has CKD stage G2.
questions.explanation: G1 and G2 count as CKD only when there is other evidence of kidney damage such as albuminuria, haematuria or structural abnormality. With a mildly reduced eGFR alone and no other marker, the patient does not meet the diagnosis.
